paragraphs.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
paragraphs.text: So we're at version 1.0 of The Layered Web, The Desirable Properties of a Meta Layer. It is an actual book. It'd probably be better to call it a tome, because it's almost 800 pages, last time I looked. There's a lot there, and in fact, it's very much a shared achievement. Over 70 people made contributions to the book, plus we had about 20 people who also helped edit it. It is truly a collective process that we've gone through. Anyone could submit a contribution to the book, and we had a number of different co-editors per chapter, and we needed two votes to move them on. We also had a steering committee. I would love to just shout out to Phahsa, Michelle, Layla. And who else was on the steering committee? I'm gonna remember in a second.

paragraphs.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
paragraphs.text: So today is the soft launch, November 13th. This is a initiative of the Meta Layer Initiative. My name is Daveed Benjamin. I'm the founder of Bridgit.io, as well as the Meta Layer Initiative. Let's get into it.

paragraphs.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
paragraphs.text: So, as I… alluded to earlier, this has been in process for over 2 years.

paragraphs.speaker: Daveed Benjamin
paragraphs.text: And so we're thinking of this as a North Star. It's really a community-authored North Star for what an open, trustworthy and safe, layered web would… would be like. And so we've, we've, essentially put together a lot of ideas, critiques, revisions, and they've come together into a living book. This is version 1.0, and it's just the beginning of this book. It's meant to be a living book. So how did we arrive here? Well, we started with an open inquiry. We're to create this new web. what do we want it to do? What should it do? How should it protect us? What should it enable us to do? And then we had, several different periods, 3 different periods where people could provide input. We called them calls for input. The last one, we actually kind of branded it the Desirable Properties Challenge, but it was just the third of our calls for input.
